title: Cap. VII tip: Garissoles book — prior/posterior manuscripts; digression; Rom. 5 only proves consequent
pass_a_gloss: Chapter Seven: if Garissoles's arguments prove any imputation of Adam's first sin, it is only mediate or consequent. So stood Maresius's arguments. In 1648 at Montauban came out Garissoles's Explanation and Defense of the Charenton Synodical Decree on imputing Adam's first sin, dedicated to the Zurich, Bern, Basel, and Schaffhausen leaders, among whom he scattered much about unnamed persons and complained of things Placeus thinks better left unsaid for truth, peace, and Garissoles's own honor. Those so publicly accused before such men would not have failed themselves unless they preferred the church's peace to their reputation. But because that great man was taken from the church by early death — which Placeus deeply mourns — Placeus wants to spare his memory as far as he can. Setting aside the dedicatory letter, Garissoles nearly spends the whole book refuting two manuscripts and Placeus's theses. He calls one manuscript prior and the other posterior — Placeus thinks because one was written before the National Synod and one after. The prior, a few months before the Synod, its author had poured out almost on the spot when asked by an elderly pastor friend, and sent his autograph with no copy kept, shared with no colleague or friend, and never seen again by himself, because the courier pressed. So if copies spread, it was from the addressee or from Garissoles, with whom that man had shared it. Neither the author nor Placeus has it now, and Placeus does not know who does — so he cannot compare it with Garissoles's refutation. The posterior manuscript Placeus wrote with a hasty pen at the start of 1647, merely answering another manuscript opposed to his Theses by a friend venerable for age, teaching, and office, who sent it for a swift reply if Placeus did not rest in it. Placeus obeyed and answered. That answer reached Garissoles, who thought a private manuscript should be refuted in print before the Swiss who may never even have heard of it; had he published it with his refutation for those amplest men to read, they could easily have judged the whole cause. Instead he chose to keep his Adversary — if one who wished not even to offend him by a word should be called Adversary — shut within private walls, as if restrained by a dock put in, while outdoors before illustrious men he accused him most heavily and tried the whole cause against him. He cites the two manuscripts as if by one author, though he knew Placeus authored only the later, as he hints in one or two places. And though the later manuscript was distributed into fourteen chapters, he scatters extracts without marking the chapter, so you cannot tell which manuscript or chapter he quotes — which gave Placeus much trouble comparing the later manuscript (he lacks the prior) with the refutation. In that manuscript Placeus had carefully set the state of the question, then dissolved his opponent's arguments for immediate imputation from Scripture, reason, and Fathers and Reformers, and sprinkled his answer with reasons against that imputation as occasion offered. Garissoles fiercely attacked that state-of-question, neglected it, attributed to Placeus a view Placeus does not own, and fought it while inserting Placeus's replies or reasons to refute them. The opponent's arguments are best weighed from that later manuscript; Garissoles's are the same or of like weight. Placeus will still extract what he can and show they do not help antecedent imputation. Having set the question-state not as Placeus wished but against Placeus's words and mind, without any distinction of imputation, and seeing antecedent or immediate imputation cannot be proved by itself, Garissoles digressed through chapters 4–7 to prove in general that imputing another's sin is not unjust. That is first more an answer to the objection that antecedent imputation of Adam's first sin seems to fight justice, than a positive proof; and next it proves what Placeus does not deny — for anyone who owns mediate or consequent imputation of another's sin already grants some such imputation is not unjust. The need was not a generic proof but a specific proof of antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's sin, which is altogether impossible. From 'some imputation of another's sin is not unjust' it does not follow that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all posterity before hereditary corruption — no more than any other alien sin's imputation. Setting that digression aside, chapter 8 offers arguments from Romans 5:12ff; but those prove only imputation that follows hereditary corruption — Garissoles himself admits it (ch. 8 §3 p. 206), as Placeus noted above. And since they are drawn from the Apostle's comparison of Christ and Adam, one reply meets them all: the likeness is in the thing, not in the mode of the thing — a reply Placeus learned not from Socinus but from the Apostle (Romans 5:15–16), from Calvin on Romans 5:17, and from Rivetus, who says the argument does not force inherent qualities: it only proves we have righteousness in Christ as injustice in Adam; the comparison is of causes, not of the mode of communication — Adam's sin by generation, Christ's righteousness by imputation.
pass_b_english: Chapter Seven. If the Arguments of D. Garissoles prove any imputation of Adam's first sin, that it is only mediate or consequent.

I. So stood the arguments of D. Maresius. There was published at Montauban in the year 1648 An Explanation and Defense of the Synodical Decree of Charenton On the Imputation of Adam's first sin, by Antoine Garissoles, minister of the Word of God in the Church and Academy of Montauban, and Professor of Sacred Theology; dedicated to the most ample Presidents and supreme Scholarchs of the Churches and Academies of Zurich, Bern, Basel, and Schaffhausen, among whom he scattered many things about certain persons whom he does not name, and complains of things which, if I understand anything, rather ought to have been silenced for the sake of truth and peace, and of his own honor. Those who were so publicly accused before such great men would by no means have failed themselves, unless they had preferred to consult the peace and tranquility of the Church rather than their own reputation. But because (which grieves me exceedingly) that great man was snatched from the Church by an early death, I desire that his memory be spared as far as I can.

II. The dedicatory Epistle therefore set aside, he nearly in the whole book studied to refute two certain manuscripts, and Placeus's theses. Of those Manuscripts he calls one prior, the other posterior, I believe because one was written before the National Synod, the other after. The prior, a few months before the National Synod, its author, asked by a pastor friend old enough, had poured out as it were on the spot, and had sent his autograph to him, because the courier was pressing, with no copy retained, nor shared with any colleague or friend, nor afterward seen by himself in any way. And so if any copies of it have been scattered, that must have been done either by him to whom it had been sent, or by D. Garissoles himself, with whom that man had shared it. That manuscript certainly neither its own author has, nor Placeus, and who has any copy of it now wholly escapes me. And so I cannot in any way compare it with D. Garissoles's refutation.

As to the later manuscript, it was written by Placeus with a hastening pen at the beginning of the year 1647, and is nothing but a reply to another manuscript opposed to his own Theses, composed by a certain friend venerable to him for age and doctrine and office, and sent to him that he might reply quickly if he did not rest in it. Placeus obeyed him, and replied. That reply came to D. Garissoles's hands. He thought that that manuscript and private writing, together with that prior manuscript, ought to be refuted by him publicly, in a book printed, and before the Reverend Swiss, who perhaps had not received even by hearsay anything about it: which, if he had published together with his refutation, and had set it before those most ample men to be read, it would have been most easy for them to pass judgment on this whole cause. But it pleased the learned man to keep his Adversary (if yet he is to be called Adversary who desired to offend him not even by a word) shut within private walls, and as it were to restrain him by a dock put in, while outdoors, with all hearing, before most illustrious men, he accused him most heavily, and disputed that whole cause against him.

And he so cites those two manuscripts as if they had been written by the same author, when yet he was not unaware that Placeus was author of the later only; which he also hints not obscurely in one or two places. And when this later manuscript had been distributed into fourteen chapters, he scatters particles extracted from it almost everywhere, with the chapter never marked, so that you do not know from which manuscript, or chapter of the manuscript, that which he cites and refutes has been excerpted: which matter gave me very much trouble when comparing the later manuscript (for that prior one, as I said, I neither have, nor know whence I could have it) with its refutation.

But since in that manuscript Placeus had first constituted the state of the question very accurately, then had dissolved his arguments for the immediate imputation of Adam's sin with whom he was disputing, drawn from Scripture, from reason, from the testimonies of the Fathers and of the Reformers, and had sprinkled his own reply with various reasons against that imputation as occasion offered, D. Garissoles vehemently harassed that constitution and exposition of the state of the question, and when that was neglected attributed to Placeus a judgment which he does not own, and so opposed it with arguments that he everywhere inserted some replies or reasons of Placeus and studied to refute them. But how much force those arguments have to which Placeus was replying can be known from nowhere better than from that later manuscript, in which they have been carefully and with greatest faithfulness recalled to the examination of reason. But D. Garissoles's arguments are either the same as those, or, if they differ from them somehow in words and in the manner of proposing, yet the weight is nearly the same, so that they can scarcely be exempted from a comparison and contention of that Manuscript with D. Garissoles's book. I will nevertheless exempt them as far as I can, and will set them before my reader in this place, that he may see that they help antecedent imputation nothing.

He therefore, having constituted the state of the question not as Placeus wished, but as he himself wished against Placeus's words and mind, without any distinction of imputation, since he understood well enough that antecedent or immediate imputation can in no way be proved by itself, at once digressed through four whole chapters, 4, 5, 6, and 7, to prove in general that the imputation of another's sin is not unjust. Which first is not so much to argue as to answer an Argument by which the antecedent imputation of Adam's first sin is attacked, drawn from this, that it seems to fight with justice. Next he proves what Placeus does not deny. For he who acknowledges a mediate or consequent imputation of another's sin certainly confesses that some imputation of another's sin is not unjust. Therefore that was not to be proved in general concerning the imputation of another's sin; for it is clear that there can be both a just and an unjust one; but in species concerning such an imputation as the antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's sin is posited to be. Which is indeed altogether impossible to prove. But whatever it be — for now I do not wish to digress with the learned man — this is no consequence: Some imputation of another's sin is not unjust; Therefore Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all his posterity, and that by an imputation preceding hereditary corruption. For from that antecedent there does not follow such an imputation of such a sin, namely Adam's first actual sin, namely an antecedent one, any more than any imputation whatever of any other alien sin, whether of Adam himself or of other Patriarchs.

That digression therefore dismissed, in chapter 8 he brings forth certain Arguments from chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Romans, verses 12 and following. But those arguments prove only an imputation which follows hereditary corruption. First he himself confesses it, chapter 8, section 3, page 206, and elsewhere, as has been observed by us above in chapter 4, page 21, and in the last chapter, page 35.

Next, since they are drawn from the comparison which the Apostle institutes between Christ and Adam, one reply could be set against them all, namely that the likeness is in the thing only, not in the mode of the thing. Which reply Placeus did not learn from Socinus, but from the Apostle, Romans 5:15–16, from Calvin's Commentary on Romans 5:17, and, to omit others, from the most distinguished theologian Andreas Rivetus, whose words these are in the Catholic Orthodox, Tractate IV, Question 2, section 18: There is nothing in this argument, however, that forces us to acknowledge a necessity of inhering qualities. For this only can be proved, that we have righteousness in Christ, just as injustice in Adam. But it will be a comparison of causes, not of the mode by which the thing is communicated to us. For Adam's sin is communicated to us by generation, but Christ's righteousness by imputation.
source_text:
CAPUT VII.
Si quam imputationem primi Adae peccati probant Argumenta D. Garissolii, eam nonnisi mediatam seu consequentem esse.

I. Sic se habuerunt argumenta D. Maresii. Edita est Montalbani Anno M. DC. XLVIII. Decreti Synodici Carentonensis De Imputatione primi peccati Adae explicatio et defensio, autore Ant. Garissolio in Ecclesia et Academia Montalbanensi Verbi Dei ministro, et SS. Theologiae Professore; Amplissimis Ecclesiarum et Academiarum Tigurinae, Bernensis, Basileensis, Schaphusianae Praesidibus, supremisque Scholarchis etc. dicata, apud quos de quibusdam, quos non nominat, sparsit multa, et queritur, veritatis et pacis, suique adeo ipsius honoris causa, si quid intelligo, potius tacenda. Qui apud tantos viros tam publice accusati, sibi, nisi paci et tranquillitati Ecclesiae, quam famae suae, consultum maluissent, haudquaquam defuissent. Sed quia (quod mihi vehementer dolet) praematura morte magnus ille vir ereptus Ecclesiae est, parcitum eius memoriae, quantum possum, cupio.

II. Missa igitur Epistola dedicatoria, is toto fere libro duo quaedam manuscripta, Placeique theses refellere studuit. Eorum Manuscriptorum alterum prius, alterum posterius appellat, credo quia alterum ante Synodum nationalem, alterum post scriptum fuit. Prius illud paucis ante Synodum nationalem mensibus suus auctor ab amico pastore satis grandaevo rogatus ex tempore quasi fuderat, autographumque suum, quia tabellarius urgebat, nullo retento exemplari, nec cum ullo vel collega, vel amico communicatum, nec postea a se ullo modo visum, ad eum miserat. Itaque si qua illius disseminata sunt exemplaria, id, aut ab eo, ad quem missum fuerat, aut ab ipso D. Garissolio, cum quo ille id communicaverat, factum fuisse oportuit. Illud certe nec suus autor habet, neque Placeus, et quis illius aliquod habeat exemplar, nunc quidem me prorsus fugit. Itaque non possum illud cum D. Garissolii refutatione ullo modo conferre.

Ad posterius manuscriptum quod spectat, scriptum fuit a Placeo festinanti calamo ineunte anno 1647. nihilque est nisi responsio ad aliud manuscriptum ipsius Thesibus oppositum, ab amico quodam ipsi ob aetatem, et doctrinam et munus venerandum, compositum, et ad ipsum, ut ei, si minus acquiesceret, celeriter responderet, missum. Paruit ei Placeus, et respondit. Pervenit ad manus D. Garissolii ea responsio. Putavit eam manuscriptam et privatam una cum priore illo manuscripto publice, libro typis excuso, et apud Reverendos Helvetios, qui fortasse ne fando quidem quicquam de ea acceperant, sibi esse refutandam: quam, si una cum refutatione sua vulgasset, virisque amplissimis legendam exhibuisset, facillimum fuisset eis de tota hac causa iudicium ferre. Sed placuit viro docto Adversarium suum, (si tamen Adversarius appellandus est is, qui, ne verbo quidem, eum offendere cuperet) intra privatos parietes conclusum tenere, ac velut immisso lupatho coercere, dum foris, omnibus audientibus, apud illustrissimos viros, eum gravissime accusaret, causamque istam totam adversus eum disceptaret.

Ita autem duo illa manuscripta citat, quasi ab eodem autore conscripta essent, cum tamen non ignoraret solius posterioris Placeum esse autorem; id quod etiam uno aut altero loco non obscure innuit. Et cum posterius hoc manuscriptum in capita XIV. esset distributum, extractas ex eo particulas ubique fere disseminat, capite nunquam notato; ut nescias ex quo manuscripto, vel manuscripti capite excerptum sit id quod citat et refutat: quae res mihi manuscriptum posterius (illud enim prius, ut dixi, nec habeo, nec unde habere possim scio) cum eius refutatione conferenti, plurimum dedit negotii.

Quoniam autem in eo manuscripto Placeus primum statum quaestionis constituerat perquam accurate, deinde argumenta eius pro imputatione immediata peccati Adamici quicum disputabat, a Scriptura, a ratione, a Patrum et Reformatorum testimoniis ducta dissolverat, suamque responsionem variis contra illam imputationem, ut ferebat occasio, rationibus consparserat, exagitavit D. Garissolius vehementer illam status quaestionis constitutionem atque expositionem, eaque neglecta sententiam Placeo, quam non agnoscit, ubique attribuit, eamque argumentis ita oppugnavit, ut passim aliquas vel responsiones vel rationes Placei inseruerit, et refellere studuerit. Argumenta autem illius, cui Placeus respondebat, quam vim habeant, non aliunde melius cognosci potest quam ex manuscripto illo posteriore, in quo diligenter et summa cum fide ad rationis examen sunt revocata. Argumenta vero D. Gar. vel eadem sunt cum illis, vel, si ab illis aliquo modo differunt verbis et modo proponendi, idem tamen fere est pondus, ut vix a Manuscriptorum illius cum libro D. Gar. collatione et contentione eximi possint. Eximam tamen quoad potero, et hoc in loco lectori meo sistam, ut videat ea nihil antecedentem imputationem iuvare.

Ille igitur constituto, non ut voluit Placeus, sed ut ipse contra verba et mentem Placei voluit, statu quaestionis absque ulla imputationis distinctione, quoniam satis intelligebat, imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam per se ipsam probari nullo modo posse, statim digressus est totis quatuor capitibus IV. V. VI. VII. ut probaret in genere, imputationem alieni peccati iniustam non esse. Id quod primum non tam argumentari est quam respondere Argumento, quo imputatio antecedens primi Adae peccati impugnatur, ex eo ducto, quod illa videatur cum iustitia pugnare. Deinde id probat quod Placeus non negat. Qui enim imputationem agnoscit peccati alieni mediatam seu consequentem, is certe fatetur aliquam imputationem alieni peccati iniustam non esse. Non igitur in genere probandum id erat de alieni peccati imputatione; constat enim et iustam et iniustam esse aliquam posse; sed in specie de tali imputatione, qualis ponitur esse imputatio peccati Adami antecedens seu immediata. Id quod profecto probatu prorsus impossibile est. Sed quicquid sit, nunc enim mihi non libet cum viro docto excurrere, haec nulla est consequentia: Aliqua imputatio alieni peccati non est iniusta, Ergo primum peccatum actuale Adami omnibus eius posteris imputatur, et quidem imputatione corruptionem haereditariam antecedente. Non enim ex illo antecedente consequitur magis talis peccati, nempe primi actualis Adami, talis imputatio, nimirum antecedens, quam cuiusvis alius peccati alieni, sive ipsius Adami, sive aliorum Patriarcharum quaelibet imputatio.

Missa igitur illa digressione cap. viii. Argumenta quaedam profert ex cap. v. Ep. ad Rom. vss. 12. et seqq. Sed ea argumenta non probare nisi imputationem, quae corruptionem haereditariam consequitur, Primum ipse met fatetur, cap. 8. §. 3. p. 206. et alibi, ut est a nobis observatum supra cap. 4. p. 21. et cap. proximo p. 35.

Deinde cum sint ducta a comparatione, quam instituit Apostolus inter Christum et Adamum, posset iis omnibus una responsio opponi, nimirum similitudinem in re tantum esse non in rei modo. Quam responsionem Placeus non didicit a Socino, sed ab Apostolo Rom. 5. 15. 16. a Calvino Com. in Rom. 5. 17. et, ut alios omittam, a Clariss. Theologo Andrea Riveto, cuius haec sunt verba in Catholico Orthodoxo Tract. IV. Quaest. 2. §. 18. Nihil tamen est in hoc argumento quod nos adigat ut agnoscamus necessitatem qualitatum inhaerentium. Id enim probari tantum potest, nos in Christo iustitiam habere, quemadmodum in Adamo iniustitiam. Erit autem comparatio causarum, non modi quo nobis res communicatur. Nam peccatum Adami nobis communicatur per generationem, iustitia autem Christi per imputationem.
